sectionTitle: Changes of state and the particle model

specStatements.text: The density of a material is defined by the equation:
density, ρ, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m^3
volume, V, in metres cubed, m^3
The particle model can be used to explain
Students should be able to recognise/draw simple diagrams to model the difference between solids, liquids and gases.
Students should be able to explain the differences in density between the different states of matter in terms of the arrangement of atoms or molecules.

Required practical activity 5: use appropriate apparatus to make and record the measurements needed to determine the densities of regular and irregular solid objects and liquids. Volume should be determined from the dimensions of regularly shaped objects, and by a displacement technique for irregularly shaped objects. Dimensions to be measured using appropriate apparatus such as a ruler, micrometer or Vernier callipers.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.
Students should be able to describe how, w hen substances change state (melt, freeze, boil, evaporate, condense or sublimate), mass is conserved.
Changes of state are physical changes which differ from chemical changes because the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed.

scopeNotes.statement: Volume should be determined from the dimensions of regularly shaped objects, and by a displacement technique for irregularly shaped objects.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The two routes to a volume are kept apart exactly as the specification keeps them apart. Regularly shaped objects are handled by measuring length, width and height and calculating (c14, q07, q14); irregularly shaped objects are handled only by displacement in a measuring cylinder (c15, q15). No item asks a student to obtain the volume of an irregular object from its dimensions, and no item introduces a method the specification does not name, such as weighing an object in water or applying a formula for an awkward shape.

scopeNotes.statement: Dimensions to be measured using appropriate apparatus such as a ruler, micrometer or Vernier callipers.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Questions on choosing apparatus are limited to the three instruments the specification names (c17, m17, m18, q17). No item requires a travelling microscope, a laser gauge or any other instrument outside that list, and no item asks for a resolution figure to be quoted from memory beyond the ordinary values for a millimetre rule, Vernier callipers and a micrometer.

scopeNotes.statement: AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: This is an apparatus-and-techniques label for teachers, not content a student can be asked about. It is honoured by keeping the practical items inside AT 1 - use of apparatus to make and record length, volume and mass measurements - and by never asking a student to name or number an AT skill.

scopeNotes.statement: This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: A signpost to the working scientifically and maths appendices rather than assessable content. It is honoured by keeping the arithmetic in this topic to the MS skills the practical supports - substitution into an equation, unit conversion and calculation of a mean - and by never asking a student to recite a WS or MS reference code.

concepts.definition: Density is how much mass a material packs into each unit of volume. Because it is a ratio, it belongs to the material rather than to the lump of material: a small piece and a large piece of the same metal at the same temperature have the same density.
The specification defines density by density = mass / volume. Mass goes on the top and volume on the bottom, so for a fixed mass a larger volume always means a smaller density.

In the symbol form of the equation, written as rho = m/V, rho stands for density, m stands for mass and V stands for volume. The symbols are not initials of the words, which is why they have to be learned.
The specification gives density, rho, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m^3. The unit follows straight from the equation: a mass in kilograms divided by a volume in metres cubed.
Mass, m, is measured in kilograms, kg. A balance usually reads in grams, so a reading in grams must be divided by 1000 before it is used to obtain a density in kg/m^3.
Volume, V, is measured in metres cubed, m^3. For a regular solid the volume is found by multiplying length by width by height. A volume in cm^3 must be divided by 1 000 000 to convert it to m^3.
One gram per centimetre cubed is one thousand kilograms per metre cubed, so a density in g/cm^3 is multiplied by 1000 to give kg/m^3. Water is 1.0 g/cm^3, which is 1000 kg/m^3.

The particle model pictures a substance as a very large number of tiny particles in constant motion. Their spacing and arrangement explain both the three states of matter and the differences in density between those states.
In a solid the particles are packed closely together in a fixed, regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions. A solid therefore keeps its own shape and has a fixed volume.

In a liquid the particles are still close together and touching, but the arrangement is random and the particles can move past one another. A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container.
In a gas the particles are far apart, arranged randomly and moving quickly in all directions. A gas has no fixed shape or volume and fills whatever container it is put in.

A simple diagram uses identical circles for the particles. A solid is drawn as circles touching in a regular pattern, a liquid as circles touching in a random pattern, and a gas as widely separated circles. The circles are the same size in all three diagrams.

For the same substance the particles have the same mass in every state, so density depends only on how closely they are packed. Solids and liquids have similar, high densities; a gas has a much lower density because the same particles are spread through a far larger volume.

For a regularly shaped object the mass is found on a balance and the volume is calculated from measured dimensions, for example length x width x height for a cuboid. Density is then the mass divided by that volume.

For an irregularly shaped object the volume is found by lowering it into a measuring cylinder of water, or into a displacement can, and recording the volume of water pushed out of the way. The volume of the object is the rise in level, that is the final reading minus the starting reading.

The mass of the empty measuring cylinder is recorded, a measured volume of liquid is poured in, and the cylinder is weighed again. The mass of the liquid is the difference between the two readings, and that mass is divided by the measured volume.

A ruler is suitable for lengths of a few centimetres, Vernier callipers resolve to about 0.1 mm and suit small objects, and a micrometer resolves to about 0.01 mm and suits thin wires and sheets. The instrument is chosen so that its resolution is small compared with the length being measured.
Melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing and subliming are changes of state. The particles gain or lose energy and rearrange, but no particles are created or destroyed.

concepts.term: Conservation of mass in a change of state
concepts.definition: When a substance changes state the number of particles and the mass of each particle are unchanged, so the total mass is unchanged. A balance reading only falls because gas has escaped from the container, not because mass has vanished.

A change of state is a physical change: no new substance is made, and reversing the change returns the material to its original properties. In a chemical change new substances are formed and the original properties are not recovered by simply reversing the conditions.

misconceptions.question: A large block of expanded polystyrene has a greater mass than a small steel ball bearing. Which has the greater density?
misconceptions.correct: The steel. Density is mass per unit volume, not mass by itself. Steel packs about 7800 kg into each cubic metre; expanded polystyrene packs only about 20 kg into the same volume.
misconceptions.misconception: The polystyrene, because it is the heavier object, and the heavier object must be the denser one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech heavy and dense are used as if they meant the same thing, and students meet mass long before they meet density. Comparing objects of very different sizes hides the fact that density is a ratio, so only the top of the ratio is noticed.
misconceptions.correction: Insist on comparing equal volumes. Ask which is heavier, one cubic centimetre of steel or one cubic centimetre of polystyrene. Once the volume is fixed, comparing mass is comparing density.

misconceptions.question: A bar of aluminium is cut exactly in half. What is the density of each half?
misconceptions.correct: The same as before. Both the mass and the volume are halved, and halving the top and the bottom of a fraction leaves it unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: Half of what it was, because each piece now contains only half as much material.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Density is treated as a quantity that an object owns, like mass, rather than as a ratio. Since mass obviously halves, density is assumed to halve with it.
misconceptions.correction: Write the calculation out for both halves and show that the answer is identical. Reinforce that density is a property of the material, so every piece of the same material has the same value.

misconceptions.question: Which way round is the density equation?
misconceptions.correct: Density = mass / volume. The mass is divided by the volume.
misconceptions.misconception: It does not matter which way round you divide, so you divide whichever number is larger by the smaller one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that the equation contains a division but not its direction, and arithmetic habits push them to divide the larger value by the smaller one so the answer is greater than one.
misconceptions.correction: Use the unit as the check. Density is quoted in kg/m^3, and the slash tells you kilograms are divided by metres cubed, so mass has to be on top.

misconceptions.question: How do you combine mass and volume to get density?
misconceptions.correct: You divide the mass by the volume.
misconceptions.misconception: You multiply mass by volume, because an object with more mass and more volume ought to have more density.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Multiplying is the default operation when a student can recall which two quantities are involved but not the relationship. It also matches a vague feeling that bigger means denser.
misconceptions.correction: Test any suggested version against the unit. Multiplying kilograms by metres cubed gives kg m^3, which is not the unit of density; dividing gives kg/m^3, which is.

misconceptions.question: A balance reads 250 g for a block. What value of m goes into the density equation for an answer in kg/m^3?
misconceptions.correct: 0.25 kg. The equation needs a mass in kilograms, so the reading in grams is divided by 1000.
misconceptions.misconception: You put in the weight in newtons, because mass and weight are really the same measurement.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mass and weight are used interchangeably in everyday language, and both are met in the same part of the course, so a student happily converts a balance reading into newtons and uses that instead.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the two apart by unit. The density equation takes kilograms; newtons are a force. A balance measures mass, so its reading only needs converting from grams to kilograms.

misconceptions.question: A balance reads 250 g. What is that mass in kilograms?
misconceptions.correct: 0.25 kg, found by dividing the reading by 1000.
misconceptions.misconception: It stays as 250 - only the label after the number changes when you rewrite it in kilograms.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Unit conversion is treated as relabelling rather than rescaling, especially when the student is copying the number straight into a calculator and thinking about the physics rather than the arithmetic.
misconceptions.correction: Anchor the size of the unit: a kilogram is a thousand times bigger than a gram, so the number of kilograms must be a thousand times smaller. 250 g is a quarter of a kilogram, so 0.25 kg is sensible.

misconceptions.question: Aluminium has a density of 2.7 g/cm^3. What is this in kg/m^3?
misconceptions.correct: 2700 kg/m^3. One g/cm^3 is 1000 kg/m^3, so the number is multiplied by 1000.
misconceptions.misconception: When converting g/cm^3 to kg/m^3 (or g to kg) the student scales by the wrong power of ten or the wrong way - dividing instead of multiplying, or shifting only one place - unsure how the smaller unit relates to the larger.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The student notices only the mass part of the unit and applies the g to kg conversion, forgetting that the volume unit has changed as well and by a much larger factor.
misconceptions.correction: Convert the two parts separately: 1 g becomes 0.001 kg, and 1 cm^3 becomes 0.000001 m^3. Dividing 0.001 by 0.000001 gives 1000, so multiply by 1000. Water at 1.0 g/cm^3 is 1000 kg/m^3, which is a useful check.

misconceptions.question: In the equation rho = m/V, what do m and V represent?
misconceptions.correct: m is the mass and V is the volume.
misconceptions.misconception: The letters in rho = m/V are read with their commonest physics meanings - m as metres (a length) and V as velocity - instead of mass and volume, so the wrong quantities are substituted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The same letters are used for other quantities elsewhere in the course, and m is also the abbreviation for the metre, so a student who has learned symbols by their commonest meaning misreads the equation.
misconceptions.correction: Read the symbols back from the specification's own list of quantities and units for this equation, and check the result: mass over volume gives kg/m^3, which is the unit of density.

misconceptions.question: A block measures 0.30 m by 0.20 m by 0.10 m. What is its volume?
misconceptions.correct: 0.006 m^3, found by multiplying the three dimensions together.
misconceptions.misconception: Finding a volume from measured lengths, the student combines the three dimensions wrongly - adding them, multiplying only two, or multiplying all three but dropping the decimal factors - so the result has the wrong size.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Adding is easier than multiplying three decimals, and the student is not checking the unit of the answer. The idea that volume is a product of three lengths has been learned as a rule rather than understood.
misconceptions.correction: Check the unit produced by the operation. Adding metres to metres gives metres, not metres cubed. Only multiplying three lengths gives m^3.

misconceptions.question: Why does a substance take up more room as a gas than as a liquid?
misconceptions.correct: The particles move much further apart. The particles themselves are unchanged in size and mass.
misconceptions.misconception: The particles themselves swell up when they are heated, and that is why the gas fills a bigger space.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Expansion is an observed fact about the material, and the simplest picture of it is that everything in the material gets bigger, including the particles. Diagrams that draw gas particles larger than solid particles reinforce this.
misconceptions.correction: Draw all three states with identical circles and change only the spacing. Point out that the mass of each particle is fixed, so only the spacing can change the density.

misconceptions.question: How closely packed are the particles in a liquid?
misconceptions.correct: About as closely as in a solid. They touch one another but are arranged randomly and can slide past each other.
misconceptions.misconception: About halfway between a solid and a gas, so a liquid should be drawn with clear gaps between the particles.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The order solid, liquid, gas suggests an evenly spaced sequence, and many textbook diagrams exaggerate the gaps in a liquid to show that its particles can move.
misconceptions.correction: Compare real densities: liquid water is 1000 kg/m^3 and ice is about 920 kg/m^3, while steam is well under 1 kg/m^3. Liquids sit next to solids, nowhere near gases.

misconceptions.question: How should a solid be drawn in a simple particle diagram?
misconceptions.correct: As circles touching one another in a regular, repeating pattern with no gaps.
misconceptions.misconception: As a neat grid of circles with clear spaces left between them, so the pattern is easy to see.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are taught that a solid is regular and draw a grid for tidiness, spacing the circles out so the arrangement is visible. The gaps are a drawing convenience that then gets read as physics.
misconceptions.correction: Judge a diagram on two separate features: the arrangement, regular or random, and the spacing, touching or far apart. A solid must be regular and touching.

misconceptions.question: Why is the density of steam so much lower than the density of liquid water?
misconceptions.correct: The same particles are spread through a far larger volume, so each cubic metre contains far less mass.
misconceptions.misconception: The particles in a gas are smaller and lighter than the particles in the liquid, otherwise the gas could not float upwards.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gases feel weightless, so their particles are imagined to be lighter. The student is changing the mass of a particle to explain a change that is actually caused by spacing.
misconceptions.correction: Insist that steam is made of exactly the same molecules as the water it came from. Nothing about a molecule changes on boiling except how far it is from its neighbours.

misconceptions.question: Ice floats on water. What does that tell you about the density of ice?
misconceptions.correct: It is lower than the density of liquid water, because the molecules in ice are held in an open arrangement that spaces them slightly further apart.
misconceptions.misconception: When ice melts the balance reading is thought to change with the water's density or volume - judging the denser water to weigh more, or its smaller volume to weigh less - instead of mass being conserved.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The general rule that solids are denser than liquids is true for most substances and is taught as if it had no exceptions, so the floating of ice is either not noticed or explained away.
misconceptions.correction: Use the general rule but state the exception explicitly, with the numbers: ice is about 920 kg/m^3 against 1000 kg/m^3 for water, which is why it floats.

misconceptions.question: A measuring cylinder holds 50 cm^3 of water. A stone is lowered in and the level rises to 128 cm^3. What is the volume of the stone?
misconceptions.correct: 78 cm^3, the rise in the level, found by subtracting the first reading from the second.
misconceptions.misconception: In a displacement measurement the student does not subtract the starting level to get the rise; they report a single raw reading - the final or the starting one - or add the two readings together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The final reading is the number the student has just taken and it is the largest one on view, so it is copied down without asking what part of that volume is water that was already there.
misconceptions.correction: Label the readings before and after and write volume of object = final reading minus starting reading. Sketch the cylinder twice so the water that was already present is visible.

misconceptions.question: An empty measuring cylinder has a mass of 62 g. Filled to the 40 cm^3 mark with oil it has a mass of 99 g. What is the density of the oil?
misconceptions.correct: 0.93 g/cm^3. The mass of the oil alone is 99 - 62 = 37 g, and 37 / 40 = 0.93 g/cm^3.
misconceptions.misconception: Finding the mass of a liquid, the student does not subtract the empty container's mass; they use the wrong mass - the combined reading, the empty-container reading, or the sum of the two - instead of the difference.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The balance shows one number and the cylinder shows another, so the student pairs them without noticing that the mass reading includes the glass, which contributes no volume to the 40 cm^3.
misconceptions.correction: Record three quantities every time: mass of empty cylinder, mass of cylinder and liquid, volume of liquid. The mass of the liquid is always the difference between the first two.

misconceptions.question: Which instrument should be used to measure the diameter of a wire about 0.4 mm across?
misconceptions.correct: A micrometer, because it resolves to about 0.01 mm, which is small compared with 0.4 mm.
misconceptions.misconception: A millimetre rule is fine, because you can see the wire and estimate the fraction of a millimetre between the marks.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A rule is the familiar instrument and estimating between marks feels reasonable. The student does not compare the resolution of the instrument with the size of the thing being measured.
misconceptions.correction: Compare resolution with measurement. A rule reading to 1 mm gives an uncertainty of more than the whole diameter; a micrometer reading to 0.01 mm gives an uncertainty of a few per cent.

misconceptions.question: Do Vernier callipers and a micrometer measure the same thing equally well?
misconceptions.correct: Both measure length, but they differ in resolution. Callipers read to about 0.1 mm and a micrometer to about 0.01 mm, so the micrometer suits the smallest lengths.
misconceptions.misconception: Any length instrument will do, because they all measure in the same unit and so all give the same answer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Instruments are grouped by the quantity they measure rather than by their precision, so resolution is treated as a detail rather than as the reason for choosing one over another.
misconceptions.correction: Quote the resolution of each instrument alongside its name, and choose the instrument whose resolution is a small fraction of the length being measured.

misconceptions.question: Water is boiled away in an open pan on a balance and the reading falls. Where has the mass gone?
misconceptions.correct: Into the air. The water has become steam that has left the pan, so it is no longer resting on the balance. No mass has been destroyed.
misconceptions.misconception: Boiling uses the water up, so that mass really has gone; the heat has destroyed it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday phrase boiled dry and the invisibility of water vapour make it look as though the water has ceased to exist. Conservation of mass is easy to state and hard to believe when the product cannot be seen.
misconceptions.correction: Repeat the change in a sealed container on a balance. The reading does not move, which shows the mass is still present and only its location changed in the open pan.

misconceptions.question: A dish of solid carbon dioxide sublimes in the open and the balance reading falls to zero. Has mass been lost from the universe?
misconceptions.correct: No. The carbon dioxide gas has spread into the room. Gases do have mass; a cubic metre of air has a mass of about 1.2 kg.
misconceptions.misconception: Gases have no mass at all, so once the solid has become a gas there is nothing left to weigh.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gases cannot be seen, felt or held, and everyday experience offers no sense of their weight, so students treat them as nothing rather than as matter that is thinly spread.
misconceptions.correction: Give gases a mass in numbers: the air in a small bedroom has a mass of around 40 kg. Then weigh a sealed flask before and after air is pumped out.

misconceptions.question: Is boiling water a chemical change?
misconceptions.correct: No, it is a physical change. Steam is still water, and cooling it gives back liquid water with all its original properties.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes, because steam looks and behaves completely differently from water, so it must be a new substance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: New appearance is taken as evidence of a new substance. A change of state alters every property a student can observe directly, so it is easy to conclude that the material itself is different.
misconceptions.correction: Apply the reversal test. Cool the steam and the original liquid comes back unchanged, which shows no new substance was ever made.

misconceptions.question: What makes a change of state a physical change rather than a chemical one?
misconceptions.correct: No new substance is formed, and reversing the change returns the material to its original properties.
misconceptions.misconception: Physical changes are simply the reversible ones, and a chemical change can never be reversed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reversibility is a useful signpost and gets promoted into the definition, even though many chemical changes, such as the reaction of hydrogen and oxygen, can be reversed by other means.
misconceptions.correction: Define the difference by what is present afterwards: a physical change leaves the same substance, a chemical change makes new ones. Reversibility is then a consequence, not the test itself.

misconceptions.question: Which unit does the AQA specification use for density in the equation rho = m/V?
misconceptions.correct: Kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³, because the specification uses mass in kilograms and volume in metres cubed.
misconceptions.misconception: Density is measured in grams per centimetre cubed, g/cm³ - that is the density unit, because it is the one always used in lessons and data tables.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Classroom practicals and chemistry data tables almost always quote densities in g/cm³, because blocks and liquids are measured in grams and centimetres, so students take the familiar unit to be the standard one.
misconceptions.correction: g/cm³ is a valid everyday unit, but the specification's standard unit is kg/m³, built from the SI units kilogram and metre. Values can be converted: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³, so water is 1 g/cm³ or 1000 kg/m³.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is the definition of the density of a material?

options.text: The volume the sample fills divided by its own mass.
options.rationale: The division is the right way up for the student but upside down for physics. Anyone who remembers only that a division is involved can end up here.

options.text: The mass of the sample multiplied by the volume.
options.rationale: Half-remembering the equation as a product. It also fails the unit test, since kg multiplied by m^3 is not kg/m^3.

options.text: The mass of the sample divided by its volume.
options.rationale: This is the definition the specification gives: density = mass / volume.

options.text: The total mass the sample happens to have.
options.rationale: Density is treated as another word for mass, which is why a big heavy object is assumed to be the dense one.

mcqs.stem: In the equation ρ = m/V, what do the symbols m and V stand for?

options.text: m stands for mass and V stands for volume.
options.rationale: These are the quantities the specification lists for this equation: mass, m, in kilograms and volume, V, in metres cubed.

options.text: m stands for metres and V stands for volume.
options.rationale: m is also the abbreviation for the metre, so a student reading the symbol as a unit rather than a quantity picks this.

options.text: m stands for mass and V is the speed it moves.
options.rationale: V is met as velocity elsewhere in the course, and that meaning is carried across to this equation.

options.text: m stands for the weight and V for the volume.
options.rationale: Mass and weight are used as if they were the same quantity, so the symbol on top is read as a force.

mcqs.stem: Which unit does the specification use for density?

options.text: kilograms times metres cubed, kg m³
options.rationale: This is the unit you would get from multiplying mass by volume, so it comes with the belief that density is a product.

options.text: kilograms per metre squared, kg/m²
options.rationale: Area is used in place of volume, usually by a student who has multiplied only two of the three dimensions.

options.text: kilograms per metre cubed, written kg/m³
options.rationale: The specification gives density, ρ, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m^3, which follows from dividing a mass in kg by a volume in m^3.

options.text: grams per centimetre cubed, g/cm³
options.rationale: A real unit of density and the one used in most data books, but not the unit the specification names.

mcqs.stem: A cube of steel has sides of 0.10 m and a mass of 7.8 kg. What is its density?

options.rationale: Mass has been multiplied by volume instead of divided, giving 7.8 x 0.001.

options.text: 7800 kg/m³
780 kg/m³
options.rationale: The mass has been divided by the area of one face, 0.01 m^2, rather than by the volume.

options.text: 78 kg/m³
options.rationale: The mass has been divided by a single side length, 0.10 m, so only one dimension has been used.

mcqs.stem: A liquid has a density of 800 kg/m³. What volume is occupied by 2.0 kg of the liquid?

options.rationale: Rearranging ρ = m/V gives V = m/ρ = 2.0 / 800 = 0.0025 m^3.
The division is set up correctly but the decimal point is misplaced by a factor of ten, a common slip when dividing by a three-figure number.
Mass and density have been multiplied rather than divided.

options.text: 400 m³
options.rationale: The division has been done the wrong way round, 800 divided by 2.0.

mcqs.stem: Aluminium has a density of 2.7 g/cm³. What is this density in kg/m³?

options.rationale: Divided by 1000 instead of multiplied, on the grounds that a gram is smaller than a kilogram.

options.text: 2.7 kg/m³
options.rationale: The number has been left alone and only the unit label rewritten.

options.text: 2700 kg/m³
options.rationale: One g/cm^3 is 1000 kg/m^3, so 2.7 g/cm^3 x 1000 = 2700 kg/m^3.

options.text: 27 kg/m³
options.rationale: A partial conversion, multiplying by ten rather than by a thousand.

mcqs.stem: A rectangular block measures 0.30 m by 0.20 m by 0.10 m. What is its volume?

options.rationale: Only two of the three dimensions have been multiplied, which gives an area rather than a volume.
Volume of a cuboid = length x width x height = 0.30 x 0.20 x 0.10 = 0.006 m^3.

options.text: 0.6 m³
options.rationale: The three dimensions have been added instead of multiplied.

options.text: 6 m³
options.rationale: The volume has been worked out in cm^3 as 6000 and then divided by 1000, as though a cubic metre were a thousand cubic centimetres.

mcqs.stem: A balance shows the mass of a block as 250 g. Which value should be used for m to obtain a density in kg/m³?

options.text: 250 000 kg, the reading multiplied by 1000
options.rationale: The conversion has been applied in the wrong direction, making the mass a thousand times larger instead of smaller.

options.text: 250 kg, the balance reading itself
options.rationale: The reading is copied straight across, treating the change of unit as a change of label only.

options.text: 2.5 N, the weight the balance is showing
options.rationale: Mass has been converted into a force, which cannot go into a density calculation.

options.text: 0.25 kg, the reading divided by 1000
options.rationale: The equation needs mass in kilograms, and 250 g is 250 / 1000 = 0.25 kg.

mcqs.stem: A solid aluminium bar is cut exactly in half. What is the density of each half?

options.text: Half the original value, since each piece has half the mass.
options.rationale: Only the top of the ratio is tracked. Because the mass obviously halves, the density is assumed to halve too.

options.text: A quarter of the original value, since mass times volume is used.
options.rationale: m04 treats density as mass x volume; halving both mass and volume gives one quarter.

options.text: A little lower, since each half now weighs less.
options.rationale: m01 (heavier means denser): the lighter half is judged less dense, so density falls.

options.text: The same as the whole bar, because mass and volume both halve.
options.rationale: Density is a property of the material. Halving the mass and the volume together leaves the ratio unchanged.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the arrangement of particles in a solid, a liquid and a gas?

options.text: Solid: regular and touching; liquid: evenly spaced out; gas: far apart.
options.rationale: The liquid is placed halfway between a solid and a gas, a spacing suggested by the order of the three states.

options.text: Solid: small particles; liquid: larger ones; gas: the largest of all.
options.rationale: The particles themselves are made to change size, which would mean a molecule of water differs from a molecule of steam.

options.text: Solid: regular with wide gaps; liquid: random and touching; gas: random.
options.rationale: The arrangement is right but a solid is given gaps between its particles, which would make it far less dense than it is.

options.text: Solid: regular and touching; liquid: random but touching; gas: random and far apart.
options.rationale: This matches the particle model: solids and liquids both have particles in contact, and only the gas has widely separated particles.

mcqs.stem: A student is drawing simple particle diagrams. Which drawing models a liquid correctly?

options.text: Circles of one size in a neat grid, evenly spaced.
options.rationale: This is a solid drawn with gaps, and it is also the pattern many students use for a liquid.

options.text: Circles of one size touching, with no pattern.
options.rationale: In a liquid the particles are still in contact, as in a solid, but the arrangement is random so they can slide past one another.

options.text: Circles drawn larger than those in the solid diagram.
options.rationale: Particles are made to swell when the solid melts, instead of only rearranging.

options.text: Circles spread far apart and scattered across the box.
options.rationale: This is a gas. It follows from picturing a liquid as roughly halfway between a solid and a gas.

mcqs.stem: Why is the density of steam so much lower than the density of liquid water?

options.text: Its molecules are much further apart, so that mass fills more space.
options.rationale: The particle model explains density differences through spacing: the molecules are unchanged, but each cubic metre of steam holds far fewer of them.

options.text: Its molecules are lighter and smaller than those in the liquid water, too.
options.rationale: The mass of the particle is changed to explain a difference that is caused by spacing alone.

options.text: Some of the water's mass is destroyed when the liquid is boiled away.
options.rationale: Mass is treated as something boiling can use up, which would break conservation of mass.

options.text: Each molecule swells up as it is heated, so the steam weighs less.
options.rationale: Heating is imagined to enlarge the particles themselves rather than push them apart.

mcqs.stem: Ice floats on liquid water. What does this show about ice, and why?

options.text: It is less dense, because its molecules are held slightly further apart.
options.rationale: Water is unusual: freezing locks the molecules into an open arrangement, so the same mass occupies a larger volume and the density falls to about 920 kg/m^3.

options.text: It is denser, because the solid state of a substance is always the denser one.
options.rationale: The general rule that solids are denser than their liquids is applied without allowing for the exception that is being described.

options.text: It is lighter, because a little mass is lost as the water freezes.
options.rationale: Mass is treated as something that can disappear during a change of state.

options.text: It has smaller molecules than water, which is what makes it rise.
options.rationale: The size of the molecule is changed instead of its spacing.

mcqs.stem: A student is finding the density of a rectangular metal block. Which measurements are needed?

options.text: The mass from a balance, and the length of one side from a ruler.
options.rationale: One dimension gives a length, not a volume; this would give an answer in kg/m rather than kg/m^3.

options.text: The mass from a balance, and the length, width and height from a ruler.
options.rationale: For a regularly shaped object the specification expects the volume to come from its dimensions, so all three lengths are needed along with the mass.

options.text: The mass from a balance, and the area of one face from a ruler.
options.rationale: Two dimensions give an area, so dividing by it produces kg/m^2 rather than a density.

options.text: The weight in newtons, and the three dimensions from a ruler.
options.rationale: A force has been substituted for the mass, which the density equation cannot take.

mcqs.stem: A measuring cylinder holds 50 cm³ of water. A stone is lowered in and the level rises to 128 cm³. What is the volume of the stone?

options.text: 178 cm³, the two cylinder readings added
options.rationale: The readings are combined by addition, which counts the original water twice over.

options.text: 128 cm³, the final reading on the cylinder
options.rationale: The largest number on view is copied down, ignoring the 50 cm^3 of water that was already in the cylinder.

options.text: 78 cm³, the rise in the water level
options.rationale: The volume of an irregular object is the volume of water it displaces, which is the final reading minus the starting reading: 128 - 50 = 78 cm^3.

options.text: 50 cm³, the water already in the cylinder
options.rationale: The starting reading is taken as the answer, confusing the water present with the space the stone takes up.

mcqs.stem: A student measures the density of cooking oil with a measuring cylinder on a balance. Which mass is divided by the volume of oil?

options.text: The mass of the measuring cylinder once the oil has been poured in.
options.rationale: The balance reading is used as it stands, so the mass of the glass is counted as though it were oil.

options.text: The mass of cylinder and oil minus the mass of the empty cylinder.
options.rationale: Only the oil occupies the measured volume, so the mass of the glass must be subtracted before dividing.

options.text: The mass of the empty measuring cylinder before the oil is added.
options.rationale: The wrong one of the two readings is chosen; this mass belongs to the glass alone.

options.text: The mass of the empty cylinder added to the mass of cylinder and oil.
options.rationale: The two readings are added instead of subtracted, which counts the glass twice.

mcqs.stem: Which instrument is most suitable for measuring the diameter of a copper wire about 0.4 mm across?

options.text: Vernier callipers, since they read in mm too.
options.rationale: Callipers are a genuine precision instrument, but a resolution of 0.1 mm is a quarter of the diameter being measured.

options.text: A millimetre rule, estimated by eye.
options.rationale: A rule reading to 1 mm cannot resolve a diameter smaller than one of its divisions.

options.text: A micrometer, reading to 0.01 mm.
options.rationale: The resolution needs to be small compared with 0.4 mm. A micrometer reading to 0.01 mm measures the diameter to about two per cent.

options.text: Any of them, since all read in mm.
options.rationale: Instruments are chosen by the quantity they measure rather than by their resolution.

mcqs.stem: A sealed container holds 200 g of ice. The container is left until all the ice has melted. What does the balance read now?

options.text: 200 g, because melting rearranges the particles but removes none.
options.rationale: Mass is conserved in a change of state. The container is sealed, so nothing can enter or leave.

options.text: Less than 200 g, because some of the ice gets used up as it melts.
options.rationale: Melting is treated as consuming the material, so mass is expected to disappear.

options.text: More than 200 g, since liquid water is denser than solid ice.
options.rationale: A correct fact about density is mistaken for a fact about mass; the volume falls but the mass does not change.

options.text: 100 g, since the water takes up far less room than the ice.
options.rationale: The drop in volume on melting is carried straight over to the mass reading.

mcqs.stem: Solid carbon dioxide sublimates in an open dish on a balance and the reading falls to zero. Has any mass been destroyed?

options.text: Yes, subliming uses the solid up, so that mass has gone for good now.
options.rationale: A change of state is read as the destruction of the material because the product cannot be seen.

options.text: No, but gases weigh nothing at all, so the reading had to fall away.
options.rationale: Mass is said to be conserved while gases are still treated as having none, which is self-contradictory.

options.text: Yes, because a gas is a new substance made out of that solid.
options.rationale: Sublimation is treated as a chemical change producing something new rather than the same substance in another state.

options.text: No, the gas has spread into the room and is not on the balance.
options.rationale: Sublimation is a change of state, so mass is conserved. The balance reads zero only because the carbon dioxide is no longer on the pan.

mcqs.stem: Why is boiling water classed as a physical change rather than a chemical change?

options.text: Steam is a new substance, but a very easy one to turn back.
options.rationale: The change is accepted as physical while still treating steam as a different substance from water.

options.text: Physical changes are reversible and chemical changes are not.
options.rationale: Reversibility is promoted from a consequence into the definition, which misclassifies reversible reactions.

options.text: Boiling can be undone, so it cannot be a chemical change.
options.rationale: m22 equates reversible with physical; boiling reverses, so it is judged non-chemical.

options.text: The steam is still water; cooling gives the liquid back.
options.rationale: In a physical change no new substance is formed, and reversing the change recovers the original properties.
